questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is launching a monthly in-store injection service for a medication that Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer. The written protocol has the pharmacist complete the sale and hand the prefilled syringe to the patient at the register, has the patient carry it to the consultation room and hand it back unopened, and then has the pharmacist give the injection. The protocol assigns the patient no preparation, storage, or handling role, sets no interval between the handover and the return, and runs the same way for every patient. A staff pharmacist asks whether the protocol is acceptable. Which assessment is best?

choices.text: The formal characterization of the handover as a completed dispensing controls, so no administration restriction is engaged.
The patient's possession of the syringe makes the patient rather than the pharmacist the administering party.
The protocol is impermissible, because arranging the steps this way indirectly circumvents the administration restriction.
A valid prescription and a lawful dispensing together authorize the pharmacist to administer the medication.
Responsibility for the arrangement rests with whoever designed the protocol, not with the pharmacist following it.
